column4: The source section sets faces apart on that Day; this ayah divides them into faces that brighten and faces that darken, a direct contrast in facial outcomes.
The source section's root خ ش ع describes lowering and abasement; here, on the Day of Resurrection, voices are humbled before the Merciful, extending that stance beyond faces.
The section asks readers to look at the sky; this ayah likewise directs them to the sky above and how it was built.
The ayah pairs the built sky with earth spread out, mountains set, and growth from the ground, matching the section's sky-and-earth gaze.
The passage calls the sky and earth a reminder and insight; this adds the purpose of looking at creation in the neighboring scene at 50:6–7.
Earth is spread, mountains set, and measured growth brought forth; this develops the source section's soft, fertile-ground image.
The ayah says earth was spread out, a direct scene parallel to the section's attention to how earth lies open before the observer.
The ayah says God made earth a spread-out expanse, repeating the ground-forming scene that the section asks readers to observe.
The oath names earth and the One who spread it; this is another direct formulation of the section's spread-earth image.
Earth is spread with rivers and fruits and mountains, joining the section's ground, water, and fertility details in one scene.
Mountains anchor the earth, water descends from the sky, and good plants grow; this joins the source section's sky, ground, and fertility images.
The source section's dictionary sense of samāʾ includes cloud and rain; this ayah shows piled clouds, rain, and hail from the sky.
Garden rivers of unaltered water stand in the same ayah against boiling water that cuts the insides, compressing the source section's running-spring and hot-spring reversal.
The source section's dictionary form for good earth ends in طيبة; this ayah describes Sheba's fertile settlement as بلدة طيبة beside its paired gardens.
After the good land at 34:15, a flood replaces its gardens with bitter, sparse growth, showing water's provision turned into loss.
The source section names عين as a spring; this ayah says God made gardens and brought forth springs in the earth.
After the hot-water punishment in this passage, the God-fearing are in Gardens and springs, a clear reversal of the source section's boiling spring.
The source section's عين is a spring; here the righteous pass a cup of drink from a flowing spring, the life-giving counterpart to boiling water.
The Garden's people receive cups and a drink from a flowing spring, matching the source section's عين جارية and drink provision.
Water bursts from stone as twelve springs, a concrete spring scene matching the source section's flowing عين.
Even stones split and release water or gush out rivers; this links the source section's dry, lowered ground to the surprising emergence of flowing water.
The source section's root س ق ي means giving drink; Moses reaches water where people water their flocks, an ordinary provision scene opposite the harmful drink.
Moses waters the two women's flock, then sits in shade; this completes the source section's giving-drink root in a scene of labor followed by relief.
After the hot drink and the thirsty-camel comparison, this ayah calls it their welcome on the Day of Recompense, identifying the drink as punitive provision.
